sections.heading: Pituitary: development, hormones, tumours and water balance
sections.html:
Development and anatomy

The anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis) grows up from the roof of the primitive mouth as Rathke pouch (surface ectoderm). The posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) grows down from the floor of the diencephalon (neuroectoderm) and is really a bundle of hypothalamic axon terminals. The anterior lobe has no direct arterial supply of note: it receives hypothalamic releasing hormones through the low-pressure hypophyseal portal veins of the stalk, which is why it is vulnerable to ischemia and why stalk damage changes its output. The gland sits in the sella turcica under the optic chiasm, with the cavernous sinuses (cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI, and the internal carotid artery) on each side.

[[figure:s23c-fig150501-1]]

Hormones and signalling

HormoneCellReceptor signallingMain control
GHSomatotroph (acidophil)Cytokine-type receptor, JAK2-STATGHRH up; somatostatin and IGF-1 down; sleep, exercise, hypoglycemia raise it; hyperglycemia lowers it
ProlactinLactotroph (acidophil)Cytokine-type receptor, JAK2-STATTonic inhibition by dopamine (D2) from the arcuate nucleus; TRH and estrogen raise it
ACTHCorticotroph (basophil), cut from POMCMC2R, cAMPCRH and ADH up; cortisol down
TSH, LH, FSHBasophils; share an alpha subunit with hCGGs, cAMPTRH; pulsatile GnRH; sex steroids and inhibin feed back
ADH (vasopressin)Hypothalamic neurons, released from posterior lobeV2 (Gs, cAMP, aquaporin-2) in collecting duct; V1 (Gq) on vesselsPlasma osmolality (main), volume and pressure, nausea, pain
OxytocinHypothalamic neurons, posterior lobeGqSuckling, cervical stretch

Pituitary adenomas

Most are benign monoclonal tumours. Microadenomas are under 1 cm; macroadenomas are 1 cm or more and cause mass effects:

  • Bitemporal hemianopia from pressure on the crossing nasal retinal fibres in the chiasm.
  • Hypopituitarism, typically losing GH and gonadotropins first, then TSH, then ACTH.
  • Stalk effect: compression of the stalk stops dopamine reaching the lactotrophs, so prolactin rises modestly (usually below about 100 ng/mL) even though the tumour does not make prolactin.
  • Lateral spread into the cavernous sinus causes diplopia from cranial nerve palsies.

Prolactinoma is the commonest functioning adenoma. Prolactin suppresses GnRH, giving amenorrhea, infertility and galactorrhea in women, and low libido, erectile dysfunction and infertility in men (who present later, often with macroadenomas). Dopamine agonists (cabergoline, bromocriptine) act on D2 receptors to cut secretion and shrink the tumour.

Somatotroph adenoma causes gigantism if it starts before the epiphyses close and acromegaly after: coarse features, frontal bossing, prognathism, widened tooth gaps, large hands and feet, carpal tunnel syndrome, sweating, sleep apnea, insulin resistance, hypertension and cardiomyopathy, arthropathy and colonic polyps. Many tumours carry activating GNAS mutations (constitutive Gs signalling); McCune-Albright syndrome is the mosaic form. Treatment options by mechanism: somatostatin receptor ligands (octreotide, lanreotide, pasireotide) reduce GH release; pegvisomant blocks the GH receptor, so IGF-1 falls while GH rises (monitor IGF-1, not GH).

Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke pouch remnants. It is the commonest supratentorial tumour of childhood that affects the pituitary, with a second peak in older adults. It is suprasellar, cystic and often calcified, filled with dark, oily fluid. The adamantinomatous (childhood) type has beta-catenin (CTNNB1) mutations and wet keratin; the papillary (adult) type carries BRAF V600E. It causes headache, bitemporal field loss, growth failure, diabetes insipidus and, after surgery, hypothalamic obesity.

Ischemia: Sheehan syndrome and apoplexy

In pregnancy the anterior lobe nearly doubles in size (lactotroph hyperplasia) but its portal blood supply does not. Severe postpartum hemorrhage with hypotension can then cause ischemic necrosis (Sheehan syndrome). The first sign is often failure to lactate, followed by no return of menses, fatigue, hypotension and hyponatremia from cortisol and thyroid deficiency. Pituitary apoplexy is sudden hemorrhage or infarction of an adenoma: thunderclap headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia and acute adrenal insufficiency.

Water balance

Central diabetes insipidus (now also called AVP deficiency) is lack of ADH; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (AVP resistance) is a collecting duct that cannot respond (V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 variants, lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia). Both give large volumes of dilute urine. SIADH is the opposite: ADH secreted despite low plasma osmolality, so free water is retained. The patient is clinically euvolemic because volume expansion triggers natriuresis (natriuretic peptides up, renin-aldosterone down), so urine sodium is high. Causes include small cell lung cancer (ectopic ADH), CNS disease, lung disease, drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, vincristine), pain, nausea and postoperative states.

Exam trap: a modestly raised prolactin with a large sellar mass is not necessarily a prolactinoma. Prolactinomas big enough to compress the chiasm usually raise prolactin far higher. Think stalk effect from a nonfunctioning adenoma, and remember the opposite pitfall, the hook effect: with a giant prolactinoma, very high prolactin can saturate the assay and read falsely low unless the sample is diluted.

Memory aid (Naadi): the pituitary loses its jobs in the order "Grow, Get pregnant, Thyroid, Then stress": GH, gonadotropins, TSH, then ACTH.

sections.heading: Pituitary tumours, apoplexy and hypopituitarism: diagnosis and management
sections.html:
Approach to a sellar mass

Image with pituitary-protocol MRI. Test every patient with a macroadenoma for both hormone excess (prolactin, IGF-1, and a cortisol excess screen if Cushing features) and deficiency (8 AM cortisol, free T4 with TSH, LH, FSH and testosterone or estradiol). Check formal visual fields when the mass reaches the chiasm. An incidental microadenoma that secretes nothing is followed with repeat MRI; a nonfunctioning macroadenoma with visual loss goes to transsphenoidal surgery.

Hyperprolactinemia

CauseClue
Pregnancy, lactationAlways exclude pregnancy first
Drugs that block dopamineRisperidone, haloperidol, metoclopramide, domperidone; also verapamil, opioids; onset follows the drug
Primary hypothyroidismHigh TRH stimulates lactotrophs; the pituitary may enlarge (thyrotroph hyperplasia) and shrinks on levothyroxine
Kidney failure, cirrhosisReduced clearance
Stalk compressionNonfunctioning macroadenoma, craniopharyngioma; prolactin usually below about 100 ng/mL
ProlactinomaLevel roughly parallels tumour size
MacroprolactinBig, inactive prolactin-IgG complexes; high level, no symptoms

For a suspected drug cause, the safest step is to stop or switch the drug (for example from risperidone to aripiprazole, with the psychiatrist) and repeat the level; image if prolactin stays high or the drug cannot be changed.

Prolactinoma treatment: a dopamine agonist, usually cabergoline, is first line for symptomatic micro- and macroadenomas, even with visual field loss, because it shrinks most tumours within weeks. Surgery is for intolerance, resistance or apoplexy. An asymptomatic microadenoma in a woman who does not want pregnancy can simply be watched (or treated with a combined hormonal contraceptive for estrogen replacement). In pregnancy, a microadenoma rarely grows, and the agonist is usually stopped once pregnancy is confirmed; macroadenomas need closer follow-up with visual fields.

Acromegaly

  • Screen with serum IGF-1 (age- and sex-adjusted); a single GH level is useless because GH is pulsatile.
  • Confirm when IGF-1 is high or equivocal with an oral glucose tolerance test: GH fails to suppress (to below about 1 ng/mL).
  • Then pituitary MRI. Look for complications: colonoscopy, echocardiography, sleep study, glucose, blood pressure.
  • Treat with transsphenoidal surgery; if disease persists, a somatostatin receptor ligand (octreotide, lanreotide), pegvisomant, or a dopamine agonist for mild cases; radiotherapy for resistant tumours. Cardiovascular disease is the main cause of excess mortality.

Pituitary apoplexy

Sudden severe headache, vomiting, visual loss or ophthalmoplegia, meningism and hypotension in a patient with (often unknown) adenoma. Give stress-dose intravenous hydrocortisone immediately, before imaging results if necessary, because acute ACTH loss can kill. MRI (or CT if MRI is not available) confirms it; neurosurgical decompression is for severe or worsening visual loss or reduced consciousness.

Hypopituitarism

  • Causes: tumours and their treatment (surgery, radiation), apoplexy, Sheehan syndrome, trauma, infiltration (sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis), hypophysitis (including immune checkpoint inhibitors), empty sella.
  • Secondary adrenal insufficiency has low or inappropriately normal ACTH with low cortisol; aldosterone is preserved (renin-angiotensin control), so hyperkalemia is absent.
  • Central hypothyroidism has a low free T4 with a low or normal TSH: follow free T4, not TSH, to adjust levothyroxine.
  • Replace cortisol before thyroid hormone. Levothyroxine speeds cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis in untreated ACTH deficiency.
  • Then sex steroids (or gonadotropins for fertility), GH in selected adults and children, and desmopressin if posterior deficiency.

Exam trap: in a patient with hypopituitarism, a normal TSH does not mean the thyroid is fine. Check free T4.

sections.heading: Polyuria, SIADH and short stature: diagnosis and management
sections.html:
Polyuria: diabetes insipidus or not?

Polyuria is more than about 3 L/day in adults. First exclude osmotic diuresis (glucose), then measure plasma and urine osmolality and sodium together.

  • Dilute urine (below about 300 mOsm/kg) with high-normal or high serum sodium suggests diabetes insipidus.
  • Dilute urine with low-normal serum sodium suggests primary polydipsia.
  • Check calcium and potassium and ask about lithium (nephrogenic causes).

A water deprivation test separates the three; it ends with a dose of desmopressin. Where available, stimulated copeptin (copeptin is cleaved from the same precursor as ADH and is stable to measure, after hypertonic saline or arginine) separates primary polydipsia from central DI more accurately, and a high baseline copeptin points to nephrogenic DI.

[[figure:s23c-fig150501-2]]
Primary polydipsiaCentral DINephrogenic DI
Serum sodium at baselineLow-normalHigh-normal or highHigh-normal or high
Urine osmolality after deprivationRises wellStays lowStays low
Rise after desmopressinSmallLarge (often more than 50%)Little or none
TreatmentReduce intake; treat the causeDesmopressin; MRI for the causeRemove the cause; low-sodium, low-protein diet, thiazide; amiloride for lithium

Once central DI is confirmed, image the hypothalamus and pituitary to find the cause (tumour, infiltration, trauma, surgery). With desmopressin, the main risk is hyponatremia, so patients should drink only to thirst.

SIADH

Diagnose SIADH only after confirming hypotonic hyponatremia (low serum osmolality) in a clinically euvolemic patient with inappropriately concentrated urine (above about 100 mOsm/kg) and urine sodium above about 30 mEq/L, and after excluding hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency and diuretics.

  • Severe symptoms (seizures, coma, vomiting with confusion): bolus 3% hypertonic saline.
  • Chronic or mild: fluid restriction first; then oral sodium chloride or urea; vaptans (V2 antagonists such as tolvaptan) in selected hospitalised patients with close sodium checks and not in liver disease.
  • Correction limit: in chronic hyponatremia raise sodium by no more than about 8 mEq/L in 24 hours in high-risk patients (alcohol use, malnutrition, hypokalemia, liver disease) and about 10–12 in others, to avoid osmotic demyelination. If correction overshoots, give free water and desmopressin to bring sodium back down.
  • Isotonic saline can make SIADH hyponatremia worse: the salt is excreted in concentrated urine and the water is kept.

Short stature and growth hormone deficiency

Familial short statureConstitutional delayGH deficiency or other disease
Growth velocityNormalNormal (dips before a late growth spurt)Low
Bone ageEqual to chronological ageDelayedDelayed
FamilyShort parents; final height near targetA parent who matured lateVariable
ActionReassureReassure; reach normal adult heightIGF-1 (and IGFBP-3), then GH stimulation testing and MRI; recombinant GH

A child whose growth velocity falls (crossing percentiles downward) needs evaluation: check thyroid function, celiac serology, blood count, metabolic panel, and in girls a karyotype for Turner syndrome. Weight falling before height suggests a nutritional or systemic cause; height falling with weight preserved suggests an endocrine cause.

Exam trap: hyponatremia with a concentrated urine is not always SIADH. Low cortisol (secondary adrenal insufficiency) gives the identical lab picture and is fixed by hydrocortisone, not fluid restriction.

Figure. Reading a water deprivation test: urine osmolality after deprivation and after desmopressin in primary polydipsia, central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (illustrative values).

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old boy has had morning headaches for 4 months and has crossed from the 50th to the 10th percentile for height. Visual field testing shows loss of the outer (temporal) half of the visual field in both eyes. MRI shows a 3-cm cystic suprasellar mass with peripheral calcification. At surgery the cyst contains thick, dark-brown oily fluid. The tumour most likely arose from remnants of which of the following embryologic structures?

options.label: B
options.html: Neural crest of the skull base

items.explanationHtml:
A calcified, cystic suprasellar mass with oily fluid in a child with growth failure and bitemporal hemianopia is a craniopharyngioma. It arises from epithelial remnants of Rathke pouch, the outpouching of oral (surface) ectoderm that forms the anterior pituitary.

Takeaway: craniopharyngioma comes from Rathke pouch remnants and is typically calcified and cystic.

whyNot.A: The infundibulum of the diencephalon forms the posterior pituitary and stalk, which gives rise to pituicytomas and gliomas, not craniopharyngiomas.
whyNot.B: Neural crest gives rise to tumours such as schwannomas and neuroblastoma, not sellar cystic epithelial tumours.
whyNot.C: Notochord remnants give chordomas, usually at the clivus or sacrum, which destroy bone rather than form oily calcified cysts.
whyNot.E: Thyroglossal duct remnants form midline neck cysts, not intracranial masses.

items.objective: Relate craniopharyngioma to its Rathke pouch origin and typical imaging.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man with acromegaly still has an elevated IGF-1 after transsphenoidal surgery and a year of a somatostatin receptor ligand. He is started on a drug that is a modified growth hormone molecule which binds the GH receptor but prevents the receptor from signalling. Which laboratory test is most appropriate to monitor the effect of this drug?
items.explanationHtml:
Pegvisomant is a GH receptor antagonist. It does not act on the tumour, so GH secretion continues and often rises (loss of IGF-1 feedback). Its effect is seen as a fall in hepatic IGF-1 production, so IGF-1 guides dosing (along with liver tests and periodic MRI).

Takeaway: on pegvisomant, monitor IGF-1; GH levels are uninterpretable.

whyNot.A: Insulin sensitivity often improves, but insulin is not used to judge disease control.
whyNot.B: GH stays high or rises because the receptor, not secretion, is blocked.
whyNot.D: Prolactin is relevant to mixed GH-prolactin tumours but does not measure pegvisomant effect.
whyNot.E: Urine free cortisol is a screen for Cushing syndrome.

items.objective: Explain why IGF-1, not GH, is used to monitor GH receptor antagonist therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has 6 months of progressive difficulty seeing cars approaching from either side and low libido. MRI shows a 2.8-cm sellar mass compressing the optic chiasm and displacing the pituitary stalk. Serum prolactin is 58 ng/mL (N = 2–18). After resection, immunostaining of the tumour is negative for prolactin and all other pituitary hormones. Which of the following best explains his raised prolactin?

options.label: A
options.html: Ectopic prolactin secretion by tumour cells

options.label: B
options.html: Interrupted dopamine delivery to normal lactotrophs

options.label: D
options.html: Stimulation of lactotrophs by high TRH

options.label: E
options.html: Tumour secretion of an estrogen-like factor

items.explanationHtml:
A nonfunctioning macroadenoma compresses the stalk and its portal vessels. Dopamine from the arcuate (tuberoinfundibular) neurons, which tonically inhibits prolactin, no longer reaches the normal lactotrophs, so prolactin rises modestly (stalk effect). A true macroprolactinoma this size would usually raise prolactin into the hundreds or thousands.

Takeaway: mild hyperprolactinemia with a large nonsecreting mass is the stalk effect.

whyNot.A: The tumour stains negative for prolactin, so it is not the source.
whyNot.C: Kidney failure raises prolactin, but nothing suggests reduced kidney function here.
whyNot.D: High TRH raises prolactin in primary hypothyroidism, which is not suggested.
whyNot.E: Pituitary adenomas do not make estrogen-like factors.

items.objective: Explain the stalk effect on prolactin through loss of dopamine inhibition.

items.stemHtml:
A 64-year-old man who smokes heavily has 2 weeks of confusion and fatigue. He appears euvolemic, with normal skin turgor and no edema. Chest CT shows a central lung mass. Laboratory studies:

TestValue
Serum sodium122 mEq/L
Serum osmolality256 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality520 mOsm/kg
Urine sodium58 mEq/L
TSH2.1 μU/mL
Cortisol, 8 AM18 μg/dL

The cause of his hyponatremia acts mainly through which of the following cellular events?

options.label: A
options.html: Activation of ENaC channels in principal cells

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibition of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb

options.label: C
options.html: Insertion of aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane of collecting duct cells

options.label: D
options.html: Opening of aquaporin-1 channels in the descending limb

options.label: E
options.html: Phospholipase C activation in vascular smooth muscle

items.explanationHtml:
Hypotonic hyponatremia with an inappropriately concentrated urine, high urine sodium and euvolemia, with normal thyroid and adrenal tests, is SIADH, here from ectopic ADH made by small cell lung cancer. ADH binds V2 receptors on collecting duct principal cells (Gs, cAMP, protein kinase A), which drives aquaporin-2 insertion into the apical membrane, so free water is reabsorbed.

Takeaway: SIADH retains free water through V2-mediated aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct.

whyNot.A: ENaC activation is the aldosterone effect; aldosterone is suppressed in SIADH.
whyNot.B: Blocking NKCC2 is the loop diuretic action, which impairs concentrating ability.
whyNot.D: Aquaporin-1 in the proximal tubule and descending limb is constitutive and not regulated by ADH.
whyNot.E: Phospholipase C activation through V1 receptors causes vasoconstriction, not water retention.

items.objective: Link SIADH to V2-receptor-mediated aquaporin-2 insertion.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman lost about 2 L of blood from uterine atony during delivery and needed transfusion of 4 units of red cells for hypotension. She is now 2 weeks postpartum and is otherwise recovering. Which of the following is most likely to be the earliest clinical sign of the injury she is at risk for?
items.explanationHtml:
The anterior pituitary enlarges during pregnancy without a matching rise in portal blood supply, so severe postpartum hemorrhage with hypotension can cause ischemic necrosis (Sheehan syndrome). Loss of prolactin makes failure to lactate the earliest sign; amenorrhea, fatigue, hypotension and hyponatremia follow.

Takeaway: postpartum hemorrhage followed by inability to breastfeed suggests Sheehan syndrome.

whyNot.B: Hyperpigmentation needs high ACTH (primary adrenal failure); in pituitary failure ACTH is low and skin is pale.
whyNot.C: Aldosterone is controlled by renin-angiotensin, so secondary adrenal insufficiency does not cause hyperkalemia.
whyNot.D: The posterior pituitary is usually spared, so diabetes insipidus is uncommon.
whyNot.E: Infarction of a normal-sized gland does not compress the chiasm.

items.objective: Recognise failure of lactation as the earliest sign of Sheehan syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has 1 year of reduced libido and erectile dysfunction, and 2 months of headaches. He bumps into door frames. Visual field testing shows bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 2.6-cm sellar mass extending up to the optic chiasm. Laboratory studies show serum prolactin 2,400 ng/mL (N = 2–18), total testosterone 140 ng/dL (N = 300–1,000), and normal free T4 and 8 AM cortisol. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
A prolactin level in the thousands with a macroadenoma is a macroprolactinoma. A dopamine agonist (cabergoline) is first-line treatment even when vision is affected: it normalises prolactin and shrinks most tumours within days to weeks, often restoring vision and testosterone. Fields and prolactin are rechecked closely; surgery is for resistance, intolerance or apoplexy.

Takeaway: prolactinomas, including macroadenomas with field loss, are treated first with a dopamine agonist.

whyNot.B: Somatostatin analogs treat GH-secreting (and TSH-secreting) adenomas, not prolactinomas.
whyNot.C: Radiation is reserved for tumours that resist drugs and surgery.
whyNot.D: Testosterone does not shrink the tumour or protect vision, and hypogonadism usually resolves when prolactin falls.
whyNot.E: Surgery is second line for prolactinomas because cabergoline works so well.

items.objective: Start a dopamine agonist for a macroprolactinoma even with visual field loss.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman with schizophrenia has had no menstrual period for 4 months and has milky nipple discharge. Her psychosis has been well controlled on risperidone, started 6 months ago. Urine hCG is negative. Serum prolactin is 92 ng/mL (N = 3–25). TSH, creatinine and liver tests are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discuss with her psychiatrist a switch to aripiprazole, then recheck prolactin

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the pituitary before any change in medication

options.label: C
options.html: Start bromocriptine and continue risperidone unchanged

options.label: D
options.html: Start cabergoline and stop risperidone today

options.label: E
options.html: Stop risperidone without a replacement and recheck prolactin

items.explanationHtml:
Her hyperprolactinemia began after starting a dopamine (D2) antagonist, and risperidone is one of the antipsychotics most likely to raise prolactin. When it is safe, the best step is to switch to a prolactin-sparing antipsychotic such as aripiprazole (a partial agonist), in agreement with her psychiatrist, and recheck prolactin. MRI is needed if prolactin stays high, or if the drug cannot be changed and onset does not match the drug.

Takeaway: suspected drug-induced hyperprolactinemia: change the drug safely and recheck before imaging.

whyNot.B: Imaging first is reasonable only when the drug cannot be changed or the timeline does not fit; it risks finding an incidental microadenoma.
whyNot.C: Dopamine agonists can oppose the antipsychotic effect and worsen psychosis; remove the cause instead.
whyNot.D: Stopping her antipsychotic abruptly risks relapse, and cabergoline is unnecessary if the cause is the drug.
whyNot.E: Stopping an antipsychotic without a replacement risks a psychotic relapse.

items.objective: Manage antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinemia by switching to a prolactin-sparing drug.

items.stemHtml:
A 38-year-old woman has 8 months of irregular menses, fatigue, weight gain, constipation and dry skin. Pregnancy test is negative.

TestValue
TSH64 μU/mL
Free T40.4 ng/dL
Prolactin48 ng/mL (N = 3–25)
Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodiesStrongly positive

MRI shows a symmetrically enlarged pituitary gland without a discrete adenoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Cabergoline, then repeat MRI in 3 months

options.label: B
options.html: Levothyroxine, then recheck prolactin and MRI

items.explanationHtml:
Long-standing primary hypothyroidism (Hashimoto thyroiditis) raises TRH, which stimulates thyrotrophs and lactotrophs. The pituitary enlarges from thyrotroph hyperplasia, and prolactin rises. Levothyroxine corrects both; the gland shrinks and prolactin normalises, so reassess after treatment.

Takeaway: check TSH in every patient with hyperprolactinemia; hypothyroidism can mimic a pituitary tumour.

whyNot.A: A dopamine agonist treats the prolactin but not the cause, and the gland enlargement is not a prolactinoma.
whyNot.C: Intravenous thyroid hormone is for myxedema coma; she is stable.
whyNot.D: Octreotide is for GH- or TSH-secreting adenomas; her TSH is high because the thyroid has failed.
whyNot.E: Biopsy is unnecessary; the enlargement is expected to regress with treatment.

items.objective: Treat pituitary hyperplasia and hyperprolactinemia caused by primary hypothyroidism with levothyroxine.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman has noticed that her rings no longer fit and her shoe size has increased over 3 years. She has new snoring, heavy sweating and bilateral hand numbness at night. Blood pressure is 152/94 mm Hg. She has frontal bossing, a widened nose and spaces between her lower teeth. Fasting glucose is 118 mg/dL. Serum IGF-1 is 3 times the upper limit of normal for her age. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Oral glucose tolerance test with serum GH measurements

items.explanationHtml:
She has the clinical picture of acromegaly with a high IGF-1. The confirmatory test is an oral glucose load: in healthy people glucose suppresses GH, but in acromegaly GH fails to fall below about 1 ng/mL. Pituitary MRI follows confirmation.

Takeaway: screen acromegaly with IGF-1, confirm with GH non-suppression after oral glucose, then MRI.

whyNot.A: Insulin-induced hypoglycemia is a stimulation test for GH deficiency, not excess.
whyNot.C: GH is secreted in pulses, so a random level can be high in healthy people and is not diagnostic.
whyNot.D: GHRH is measured only when ectopic GHRH secretion (for example a neuroendocrine tumour) is suspected after a pituitary cause is excluded.
whyNot.E: Somatostatin receptor imaging is not part of the routine diagnosis.

items.objective: Confirm acromegaly with failure of GH suppression after an oral glucose load.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man had transsphenoidal resection of a 1.8-cm GH-secreting macroadenoma 3 months ago. He feels better, but serum IGF-1 remains 1.8 times the upper limit of normal. MRI shows residual tumour invading the right cavernous sinus, which the surgeon considers unresectable. Visual fields are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Persistent acromegaly after surgery, with residual tumour in the cavernous sinus that cannot be removed, is treated medically. A long-acting somatostatin receptor ligand (octreotide or lanreotide) is the usual first choice; pegvisomant or combinations are added if IGF-1 stays high, and focused radiotherapy is reserved for resistant disease.

Takeaway: persistent acromegaly after surgery: start a somatostatin receptor ligand.

whyNot.A: Dopamine agonists help only mild disease, usually with modest IGF-1 elevation, and are not first choice here.
whyNot.C: Repeat surgery cannot reach tumour that invades the cavernous sinus.
whyNot.D: Untreated GH excess raises cardiovascular, metabolic and cancer risk; it should be controlled.
whyNot.E: Whole-brain radiation is not used; focused radiotherapy is a later option for resistant tumours.

items.objective: Treat persistent acromegaly after surgery with a somatostatin receptor ligand.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man has sudden, severe headache that started 3 hours ago, with vomiting and double vision. He has had low energy and reduced libido for a year. Temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), blood pressure 86/54 mm Hg and pulse 112/min. He has a right third nerve palsy and reduced visual acuity in both eyes. Noncontrast CT of the head shows a sellar mass with hemorrhage. Blood is drawn for cortisol, free T4 and electrolytes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Sudden headache, ophthalmoplegia and visual loss with hemorrhage into a sellar mass is pituitary apoplexy. Hypotension suggests acute ACTH deficiency, which can be fatal. Give stress-dose intravenous hydrocortisone immediately after drawing blood, with fluids, then arrange urgent neurosurgical review for decompression given the visual deficit.

Takeaway: in pituitary apoplexy, give IV hydrocortisone first.

whyNot.A: Cabergoline treats prolactinomas over weeks; it does nothing for acute adrenal crisis.
whyNot.C: Thyroid hormone before cortisol can precipitate or worsen adrenal crisis.
whyNot.D: The CT already shows the cause; lumbar puncture adds nothing and delays treatment.
whyNot.E: Waiting for results while he is hypotensive risks death from adrenal crisis.

items.objective: Give stress-dose hydrocortisone first in pituitary apoplexy.

items.stemHtml:
A 44-year-old woman had radiation therapy for a nasopharyngeal cancer 6 years ago. She now has fatigue, cold intolerance and weight gain. Blood pressure is 102/66 mm Hg.

TestValue
Sodium132 mEq/L
Potassium4.2 mEq/L
TSH1.1 μU/mL
Free T40.5 ng/dL
Cortisol, 8 AM2.1 μg/dL
ACTH8 pg/mL (N = 10–60)

Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Hydrocortisone, with levothyroxine started after it

options.label: C
options.html: Levothyroxine, with hydrocortisone if she remains tired

options.label: D
options.html: Levothyroxine and hydrocortisone started at the same high dose

items.explanationHtml:
Low free T4 with an inappropriately normal TSH, and low cortisol with a low ACTH, mean secondary hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency from radiation-induced hypopituitarism. Glucocorticoid replacement comes first: thyroid hormone raises metabolic rate and cortisol clearance and can trigger adrenal crisis if cortisol is not replaced. Levothyroxine is then started and dosed by free T4, not TSH.

Takeaway: in hypopituitarism, replace cortisol before thyroid hormone.

whyNot.A: Aldosterone is preserved in pituitary disease (renin-angiotensin control), so fludrocortisone is not needed; her potassium is normal.
whyNot.C: Starting levothyroxine first risks precipitating adrenal crisis.
whyNot.D: Starting both together still exposes her to the risk of crisis; cortisol should be established first.
whyNot.E: GH replacement is considered only after the other axes are replaced, and it is not urgent.

items.objective: Replace glucocorticoid before thyroid hormone in central hypothyroidism with ACTH deficiency.

items.stemHtml: A 14-year-old boy is brought for evaluation because he is the shortest boy in his class. He has always been at the 5th percentile for height, and his height velocity over the past 2 years has been 5 cm/year. He has no pubic hair and testicular volumes are 3 mL each. His father did not start shaving until age 17 and reached a normal adult height. Bone age radiograph shows a bone age of 12 years. Thyroid function and celiac serology are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
A steady growth velocity, delayed bone age, delayed puberty and a father who matured late are constitutional delay of growth and puberty. He has more time to grow, and adult height is usually normal. Reassurance and follow-up are appropriate; a short course of low-dose testosterone can be offered if delay causes distress.

Takeaway: normal growth velocity with delayed bone age and a family history of late puberty is constitutional delay.

whyNot.A: Stimulation testing is for children with low growth velocity or low IGF-1, not this pattern.
whyNot.B: A karyotype is mainly for girls (Turner syndrome) or boys with features of a chromosomal disorder.
whyNot.C: Pituitary imaging is for suspected GH deficiency or other features of a sellar lesion.
whyNot.E: GH is not indicated for constitutional delay.

items.objective: Recognise constitutional delay of growth and puberty and reassure.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman has 3 months of intense thirst and urinating about 7 L/day, including several times at night. She takes no medications. She has no history of psychiatric illness. Laboratory studies show serum sodium 146 mEq/L, serum osmolality 298 mOsm/kg, glucose 88 mg/dL, calcium 9.3 mg/dL, potassium 4.1 mEq/L and urine osmolality 110 mOsm/kg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: Restriction of fluid intake to 1.5 L/day at home

items.explanationHtml:
Dilute polyuria with a high-normal serum sodium and no osmotic or electrolyte cause suggests diabetes insipidus rather than primary polydipsia. The next step is a supervised water deprivation test (with desmopressin at the end), or stimulated copeptin where available, to separate central from nephrogenic DI and confirm the diagnosis before treatment.

Takeaway: confirm and classify diabetes insipidus with a supervised water deprivation test (or stimulated copeptin) before treating.

whyNot.A: Thiazides are a treatment for nephrogenic DI; giving one before a diagnosis is premature.
whyNot.B: Empiric desmopressin in someone who may have primary polydipsia risks dangerous hyponatremia.
whyNot.C: Kidney imaging does not distinguish the causes of dilute polyuria.
whyNot.D: Unsupervised fluid restriction in true DI can cause severe hypernatremia.

items.objective: Choose a supervised water deprivation test to evaluate dilute polyuria.

items.stemHtml: During the supervised test, after 7 hours without fluids she has lost 3% of her body weight. Serum sodium is 149 mEq/L and plasma osmolality 304 mOsm/kg; urine osmolality has risen only to 150 mOsm/kg. One hour after desmopressin, urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Her urine stayed dilute despite a rising plasma osmolality (no ADH effect), then concentrated by more than 50% after desmopressin, showing that her kidneys respond to ADH. That is central diabetes insipidus (AVP deficiency).

Takeaway: no concentration with dehydration plus a large rise after desmopressin means central DI.

whyNot.B: In nephrogenic DI the kidney does not respond to desmopressin, so urine stays dilute.
whyNot.C: In primary polydipsia, ADH release is intact and urine concentrates during deprivation.
whyNot.D: SIADH causes hyponatremia with concentrated urine, the opposite pattern.
whyNot.E: Osmotic diuresis gives urine osmolality near or above plasma, not 150 mOsm/kg.

items.objective: Interpret a water deprivation test showing central diabetes insipidus.

items.stemHtml: She is started on desmopressin and her symptoms resolve. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in her evaluation?

options.label: A
options.html: Genetic testing for AVP receptor 2 variants

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the hypothalamus and pituitary

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat water deprivation test in 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
Central DI that appears in adulthood without trauma or surgery needs MRI of the hypothalamus and pituitary to look for a cause: tumours (craniopharyngioma, germinoma, metastasis), infiltration (sarcoidosis, Langerhans cell histiocytosis), or lymphocytic infundibulohypophysitis. Anterior pituitary function should be tested too. Advise her to drink only to thirst to avoid hyponatremia on desmopressin.

Takeaway: new central DI needs sellar and hypothalamic MRI to find the cause.

whyNot.A: AVPR2 variants cause congenital nephrogenic DI, not central DI.
whyNot.B: Lithium causes nephrogenic DI, and she takes no medications.
whyNot.D: Repeating the test adds nothing once the diagnosis is clear and does not reveal the cause.
whyNot.E: The kidneys respond normally to desmopressin, so a kidney lesion is excluded.

items.objective: Image the hypothalamus and pituitary after diagnosing central diabetes insipidus.

cards.frontHtml: Embryologic origin of the anterior vs posterior pituitary?
cards.backHtml: Anterior: Rathke pouch (oral surface ectoderm). Posterior: diencephalon floor (neuroectoderm).

cards.frontHtml: Why does a nonfunctioning macroadenoma raise prolactin modestly?
cards.backHtml: Stalk effect: dopamine from the arcuate nucleus can no longer reach lactotrophs.

cards.frontHtml: Order in which pituitary axes usually fail with a growing mass?
cards.backHtml: GH, then LH/FSH, then TSH, then ACTH.

cards.frontHtml: Visual field defect from a pituitary macroadenoma pressing on the chiasm?
Calcified, cystic suprasellar mass with oily fluid in a child?
cards.backHtml: Craniopharyngioma, from Rathke pouch remnants (adamantinomatous type: beta-catenin mutations).
Failure to lactate after severe postpartum hemorrhage.
GH receptor antagonist; monitor IGF-1 (GH levels rise).

cards.frontHtml: Very large prolactinoma with only a modestly raised prolactin result: what assay pitfall?
cards.backHtml: Hook effect; repeat on a diluted sample.

cards.frontHtml: First-line treatment of a macroprolactinoma with visual field loss?
cards.backHtml: Cabergoline (dopamine agonist); surgery if resistant, intolerant or apoplexy.

cards.frontHtml: Acromegaly: screening test and confirmatory test?
cards.backHtml: Screen: IGF-1. Confirm: GH fails to suppress after an oral glucose load. Then MRI.
Stress-dose IV hydrocortisone, then urgent neurosurgical review.

cards.frontHtml: Hypopituitarism: which hormone is replaced first?
cards.backHtml: Cortisol, before levothyroxine (thyroid hormone can precipitate adrenal crisis).

cards.frontHtml: How do you dose levothyroxine in central hypothyroidism?
cards.backHtml: By free T4; TSH is unreliable.

cards.frontHtml: Water deprivation test: central DI pattern?
cards.backHtml: Urine stays dilute with dehydration, then rises sharply (often more than 50%) after desmopressin.
Hypotonic hyponatremia, euvolemia, urine osmolality above about 100 mOsm/kg, urine sodium above about 30 mEq/L, normal thyroid and adrenal function, no diuretics.

cards.frontHtml: Maximum sodium rise in chronic hyponatremia in a high-risk patient?
cards.backHtml: About 8 mEq/L in 24 hours, to avoid osmotic demyelination.

cards.frontHtml: Constitutional delay of growth vs familial short stature: bone age?
cards.backHtml: Constitutional delay: bone age delayed. Familial short stature: bone age equals chronological age.
